newsitem.title: GERMANY: Fidelity-MGAM fiasco bad news for funds industry.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity-MGAM fiasco bad news for funds industry.

text.p: Fidelity Investments said late on Tuesday that Morgan Grenfell's problems were bad news for the fund industry but insisted that its in-house controls ruled out the chance of Fidelity experiencing a similar problem.

Fidelity was presenting a range of new investment funds aimed at wooing the cautious German investor away from traditional savings vehicles like bond-based products and savings books into the riskier equity fund arena.
"It's bad news for the industry, obviously. It's not great publicity," said Richard Wastcoat, executive director of retail marketing in Europe at Fidelity.
Confidence in funds was dealt a blow last week when Deutsche Bank's asset management unit, Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, temporarily suspended three of its funds.
An urgent investigation into possible "irregularities" was launched in conjunction with regulators.

While refusing to comment directly on MGAM, Wastcoat said: "Any prudent organisation will look and see if there is anything to be learned from the MGAM situation. We hold ourselves to the highest standards and are aware of the need for strong control."
Germany is one of the fastest-growing markets in Europe for equity-backed investment funds, but the level of investment in equity funds is still well below the U.S. or British average.
Analysts believe that the greying population and expected changes in legislation for private pension provision mean the German market is set to expand in coming years.

As a result, fund management companies are battling feverishly to gain market share by showing that equity funds can allow an investor to manage risk while providing better returns than traditional savings vehicles.

A blow to investor confidence in the equity-backed funds industry in Germany -- at what is still the fledgling stage of market development -- could prove serious, forcing a return to the perceived security of bonds.

Responding to questions about the timing of launching a fund in the wake of the MGAM disaster, Wastcoat said: "The world has to go forward. Mutual funds have been around a long time and we have a lot of checks and balances in place."

Fidelity is also keen to avoid the "star" fund manager system, where the focus is on encouraging individual performance on a short-term basis, with the manager often receiving massive bonuses for going out on a limb.

"Our fund managers are compensated on performance over three to five years on rolling basis. Obviously fund managers have to have an incentive to outperform, but we take a long-term view to avoid fund managers making big bets. The "star" system is not something we want to encourage," he said.
Other controls include the close monitoring of holdings in unlisted securities, Wastcoat said.
The European Union requirement is that up to 10 percent of holdings can be made up of unlisted securities. Wastcoat said Fidelity's holdings in unlisted stocks are around two percent.
Fidelity says it has a five percent share of the 60-billion-mark German equity mutual funds market, which would work out at three billion marks.
It hopes to double this over coming years, but says this is unlikely to happen in next twelve months.

The German investor is younger than in Fidelity's other main markets. The average age of the British investor is 56 years of age, in the U.S it is 46 years of age. The average age of Fidelity's German investor is a youthful 35.

Its new fund range for Germany is called the Fidelity CapitalBuilder. It will be offered in deutschemarks and includes a bond-based fund, a cash fund, a fund tracking the DAX index of German shares and an international fund.
